title: Anatomy of Conjunctiva, Types of Conjunctivitis and Pterygium

questions.q: Which statement about the conjunctiva is correct?
opts: It is a transparent mucous membrane that does not cover the cornea
It is an opaque fibrous coat that covers the cornea
It is a transparent membrane that continues over the cornea
It is a mucous membrane that covers the cornea but not the sclera
questions.exp: Conjunctiva is a transparent mucous membrane. It does not cover cornea. (Book p195)

questions.q: The bulbar conjunctiva covers the ___, while the palpebral conjunctiva lines the inner surface of the ___.
questions.exp: Parts of conjunctiva: Bulbar (covers sclera); Forniceal; Palpebral (lines inner surface of eyelids). (Book p195)

questions.q: Which of the following is a part of the conjunctiva that forms the fold between the bulbar and palpebral parts?
questions.exp: Parts of conjunctiva: Bulbar (covers sclera), Forniceal, Palpebral (lines inner surface of eyelids). (Book p195)

questions.q: Match the rudimentary structure of the conjunctiva with its description — 1) Plica semilunaris  2) Caruncle  … A) Contains hair follicles  B) Represents nictitating membrane
questions.exp: Plica semilunaris: represents nictitating membrane. Caruncle: contains hair follicles. Together they are labelled rudimentary structures. (Book p195)

questions.q: True or false — 'The caruncle and the plica semilunaris are labelled as rudimentary structures of the conjunctiva.'
opts: False - only the plica semilunaris is a rudimentary structure
True - the plica semilunaris represents the nictitating membrane and the caruncle contains hair follicles
False - both are fully developed lacrimal structures
True - but the caruncle is a modified meibomian gland
questions.exp: Plica semilunaris (nicitiating membrane) and caruncle (hair follicles) are bracketed together as rudimentary structures. (Book p195)

questions.q: The outermost layer of the conjunctiva is a ___ epithelium.
questions.exp: 1. Outermost layer: epithelium (non-keratinised stratified squamous). (Book p195)

questions.q: The goblet cells of the conjunctival epithelium secrete mucin on which stimulation?
questions.exp: Goblet cells: secrete mucin (forms innermost layer of tear film) on parasympathetic stimulation. (Book p195)

questions.q: A patient's tear film is deficient in its innermost layer. Which conjunctival cells are responsible for this layer?
questions.exp: Goblet cells secrete mucin, which forms the innermost layer of the tear film. (Book p195)

questions.q: Besides goblet cells, the conjunctival epithelium contains melanocytes and which other cell?
questions.exp: The epithelium contains: a. Goblet cells b. Melanocytes c. Langerhans cells. (Book p195)

questions.q: The adenoid/lymphatic layer of the conjunctiva develops after how long?
opts: Birth - it is fully developed at birth
questions.exp: 2. Adenoid/lymphatic layer: develops after 3 months of age. (Book p195)

questions.q: The fibrous layer of the conjunctiva contains nerve fibres and ___.
questions.exp: 3. Fibrous layer: contains nerve fibres & blood vessels. (Book p195)

questions.q: The conjunctiva is the only site of ___ from the eye.
questions.exp: Lymphatic drainage: only site of lymphatic drainage from the eye. (Book p196)

questions.q: Match the direction of conjunctival lymphatic drainage with its lymph nodes — 1) Medially  2) Laterally  … A) Peri-auricular & superficial parotid lymph nodes  B) Submandibular lymph nodes
questions.exp: Drainage: medially -> submandibular lymph nodes; laterally -> peri-auricular & superficial parotid lymph nodes. (Book p196)

questions.q: Conjunctivitis is also known as:
questions.exp: Conjunctivitis: Aka eye flu. (Spring catarrh is vernal keratoconjunctivitis and Egyptian ophthalmia is trachoma.) (Book p196)

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed among the symptoms of conjunctivitis?
questions.exp: Symptoms: redness, discharge sticking to eyelids, foreign body sensation, lacrimation; itching (if allergic); pain and loss of vision (corneal involvement). (Book p196)

questions.q: A young patient with conjunctivitis complains of itching. The book attributes the itching to:
questions.exp: Symptoms include itching (if allergic); pain and loss of vision are seen with corneal involvement. (Book p196)

questions.q: A patient with conjunctivitis develops pain and loss of vision. According to the book this indicates:
questions.exp: Pain and loss of vision (LOV): corneal involvement. (Book p196)

questions.q: Which vascular sign is listed first under the signs of conjunctivitis?
questions.exp: Signs: 1. Conjunctival hyperemia (redness). (Book p196)

questions.q: Circumcorneal redness is the differential diagnosis of conjunctival redness and is seen in all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Differential diagnosis of circumcorneal redness: glaucoma, uveitis, corneal ulcer. (Book p196)

questions.q: The two clinical photographs on this page are captioned conjunctival hyperemia and ___ hyperemia.
questions.exp: Photographs: conjunctival hyperemia and circumcorneal hyperemia. Note: circumcorneal hyperemia is seen in glaucoma, uveitis and corneal ulcer. (Book p196)

questions.q: A patient has a bright red patch on the conjunctiva that resolves on its own. What treatment does the book advise for subconjunctival hemorrhage?
questions.exp: 2. Subconjunctival hemorrhage: No treatment required (resolves spontaneously in ~2 weeks). (Book p197)

questions.q: Chemosis is swelling of the ___ conjunctiva.
questions.exp: 3. Chemosis: swelling of bulbar conjunctiva. (Book p197)

questions.q: A patient reports colored halos that disappear on washing the eye, along with stickiness of the lids. The discharge responsible is described as:
questions.exp: 4. Discharge: mucopurulent/watery; causes colored halos & stickiness which resolves on washing eye. (Book p197)

questions.q: In the inflammatory reaction of the conjunctiva, papillae represent:
questions.exp: 5. Inflammatory reactions of conjunctiva: Papillae - hypertrophied vessels; Follicles - lymphoid aggregates. (Book p197)

questions.q: In contrast to papillae, conjunctival follicles are ___.
opts: Collections of eosinophils and epithelial debris
questions.exp: Follicles: lymphoid aggregates. (Papillae are hypertrophied vessels.) (Book p197)

questions.q: Match the discharge with the conjunctival reaction it indicates — 1) Mucopurulent discharge  2) Watery discharge  … A) Papillary reaction - bacterial; follicular reaction - Chlamydia  B) Papillary reaction - allergic; follicular reaction - viral
questions.exp: Etiology table: mucopurulent discharge - papillary: bacterial, follicular: Chlamydia. Watery discharge - papillary: allergic, follicular: viral. (Book p197)

questions.q: What is the most common cause of acute mucopurulent conjunctivitis?
questions.exp: Acute mucopurulent conjunctivitis: m/c cause Staphylococcus aureus. (Book p197)

questions.q: Treatment of acute mucopurulent conjunctivitis is:
questions.exp: Acute mucopurulent conjunctivitis: treatment - topical antibiotics. (Book p197)

questions.q: Acute purulent/hyperacute conjunctivitis is also known as ___.
questions.exp: Heading: Acute purulent/hyperacute conjunctivitis/Blenorrhoea. (Book p198)

questions.q: The most common cause of acute purulent/hyperacute conjunctivitis is:
questions.exp: m/c cause: Neisseria gonorrhoeae. (Book p198)

questions.q: The route of transmission of hyperacute purulent conjunctivitis is ___.
questions.exp: Route of transmission: Oculogenital. (Book p198)

questions.q: Which set of clinical features does the book list for blennorrhoea?
opts: Watery discharge, itching and cobble stone papillae
Mucopurulent discharge with redness at the intermarginal strip
Copious purulent discharge, overhanging swollen eyelids, intense pain and pre-auricular lymphadenopathy
Membrane that fuses with the epithelium and bleeds on removal
questions.exp: Clinical features: 1. Copious purulent discharge. 2. Swelling of eyelids -> overhanging. 3. Intense pain. 4. Pre-auricular lymphadenopathy. (Book p198)

questions.q: Treatment of acute purulent conjunctivitis as given in the book is:
opts: IM ceftriaxone 1 g single dose alone
IM ceftriaxone 1 g single dose, followed by oral erythromycin for 2 weeks
Topical tetracycline ointment with zinc boric drops
questions.exp: Treatment: IM Ceftriaxone 1g single dose followed by oral erythromycin x 2 weeks. (Book p198)

questions.q: A photograph on this page shows a patient with marked lid swelling and purulent discharge. Its caption is:
questions.exp: Photograph caption: Blennorrhoea. (Book p198)

questions.q: What is the most common cause of acute membranous conjunctivitis overall/in adults?
questions.exp: Acute membranous conjunctivitis - m/c cause: overall/in adults: Pneumococcus. (Book p198)

questions.q: In unimmunised children, acute membranous conjunctivitis is most commonly caused by:
questions.exp: m/c cause in unimmunised children: Corynebacterium diphtheriae. (Book p198)

questions.q: True or false — 'In membranous conjunctivitis the membrane does not fuse with the epithelium, so there is no bleeding on removal.'
opts: True - this distinguishes it from pseudomembranous conjunctivitis
False - that describes acute pseudomembranous conjunctivitis; in membranous conjunctivitis the membrane fuses with the epithelium and bleeds on removal
False - in membranous conjunctivitis the membrane fuses but still does not bleed
True - and the membrane is fixed with fibrin glue
questions.exp: Acute membranous conjunctivitis: membrane formed -> fused with epithelium -> bleeds on removal. Acute pseudomembranous conjunctivitis: membrane does not fuse with epithelium -> no bleeding on removal. (Book p198)

questions.q: The photograph on this page showing a red eye with a peeling membrane is captioned:
questions.exp: Photograph caption: Pseudomembrane peeling. (Book p198)

questions.q: Angular/diplobacillary conjunctivitis is most commonly caused by:
questions.exp: Angular/diplobacillary conjunctivitis: m/c cause moraxella lacunata/axenfeld. (Book p198)

questions.q: Excoriation in angular conjunctivitis is seen at the canthi, with ___ involvement greater than ___.
questions.exp: Clinical features: excoriation at canthi (Lateral > medial). (Book p198)

questions.q: In angular conjunctivitis, redness is seen at the:
opts: Bulbar conjunctiva over the rectus insertions
questions.exp: Clinical features: redness at intermarginal strip. (Book p198)

questions.q: A patient with angular conjunctivitis has blepharitis. In the book this refers to inflammation of the:
questions.exp: Clinical features: blepharitis (inflammation of eyelid margin). (Book p198)

questions.q: Treatment of angular conjunctivitis includes tetracycline 1% eye ointment for at least 2 weeks along with:
opts: Topical steroids, because zinc blocks proteolytic activity
Silver nitrate 1%, which blocks proteolytic activity
Zinc boric eye drops, because zinc blocks proteolytic activity
questions.exp: Treatment: tetracycline 1% eye ointment for >= 2 wks; zinc boric eye drops (zinc blocks proteolytic activity). (Book p198)

questions.q: Match the adenoviral conjunctivitis with its serovars — 1) Non-specific follicular conjunctivitis  2) Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC)  3) Pharyngoconjunctival fever (PCF)  … A) Serovars 8, 19, 37  B) Serovars 3, 4, 7  C) Serovars 1 to 11 & 19
questions.exp: Non-specific follicular conjunctivitis: serovars 1 to 11 & 19. EKC: serovars 8, 19, 37. PCF: serovars 3, 4, 7. (Book p199)

questions.q: A patient with pharyngoconjunctival fever has enlarged lymph nodes. The book records this as:
questions.exp: Pharyngoconjunctival fever (PCF): associated with preauricular lymphadenopathy. (Book p199)

questions.q: Apollo conjunctivitis is also known as acute ___ conjunctivitis, and causes hemorrhage of the palpebral and bulbar conjunctiva.
questions.exp: Apollo conjunctivitis/Acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis: hemorrhage of palpebral & bulbar conjunctiva (photograph of both red eyes). (Book p199)

questions.q: The most common cause of Apollo (acute hemorrhagic) conjunctivitis is:
questions.exp: Causes: 1. Picornavirus: Enterovirus type 70, Coxsackie A24 (m/c). 2. Adenovirus type 11. (Book p199)

questions.q: A patient has a unilateral, painless, umbilicated nodule which periodically sheds virus and produces conjunctivitis. What is the treatment advised in the book?
opts: Observation, since it never sheds virus
Surgical excision, if the cosmetic indication is positive
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum: nodule contains viral particles -> periodic shedding of virus -> conjunctivitis. Treatment: surgical excision [if cosmetic indication (+)]. (Book p199)

questions.q: The photograph on this page showing a lid nodule with a central depression is captioned:
questions.exp: Photograph caption: umbilicated nodule (molluscum contagiosum). (Book p199)

questions.q: Match the chlamydial condition with its serovars — 1) Trachoma  2) Adult inclusion conjunctivitis  3) Ophthalmia neonatorum  … A) D to K serovars  B) A, B, Ba, C serovars  C) D to K serovars and other causes
questions.exp: Adult inclusion conjunctivitis: D to K serovars. Trachoma: A, B, Ba, C serovars. Ophthalmia neonatorum: D to K serovars; other causes. (Book p199)

questions.q: Trachoma is also known as:
questions.exp: TRACHOMA aka Egyptian ophthalmia. (Book p199)

questions.q: The route of transmission of trachoma is remembered by the mnemonic ___.
questions.exp: Route of transmission: mnemonic 3F - fingers, flies, fomites. (Book p199)

questions.q: The pathology of trachoma is a Type ___ hypersensitivity reaction with active inflammation and cicatrization.
questions.exp: Pathology: Type IV hypersensitivity reaction: active inflammation + cicatrization. (Book p200)

questions.q: Trachoma is described in which age group?
questions.exp: Age group: < 10 yrs. (Book p200)

questions.q: Sago grain follicles in trachoma show which histological feature?
questions.exp: Clinical signs: 1. Sago grain follicles: necrosis & Leber; m/c site: upper palpebral conjunctiva; necrosis & Leber cells seen (photograph: sago grain follicles). (Book p200)

questions.q: Arlt's line in trachoma is a line of ___.
questions.exp: 2. Cicatricial sign: a. Arlt's line: line of cicatrization (photograph labelled lower 2/3rd and upper 1/3rd). (Book p200)

questions.q: Herbert's pits are pathognomonic of trachoma and result from healing of:
opts: Sago grain follicles of the upper tarsus
questions.exp: b. Herbert's pits: pathognomonic; d/t healing of limbal follicles (photograph label: Herbert's pits). (Book p200)

questions.q: Pannus in trachoma is:
opts: Deposition of iron in the cornea
questions.exp: c. Pannus: vascularisation of cornea superiorly. (Book p200)

questions.q: Which sequence of trachoma complications does the book give?
opts: Pannus -> trichiasis -> corneal opacity -> loss of vision
Corneal ulcer -> trichiasis -> pannus -> loss of vision
Trichiasis -> corneal ulcer -> scar formation -> loss of vision
Herbert's pits -> trichiasis -> corneal ulcer -> loss of vision
questions.exp: Complications: trichiasis (inturned eyelash) -> corneal ulcer -> scar formation -> loss of vision. (Book p200)

questions.q: Match the letter of the SAFE strategy (WHO, 1996) with its component — 1) S  2) A  3) F  4) E  … A) Azithromycin 1g  B) Surgery for inturned eyelids  C) Facial cleanliness  D) Environmental change
questions.exp: SAFE strategy (WHO, 1996): Surgery for inturned eyelids; Antibiotics: Azithromycin 1g; Facial cleanliness; Environmental change. (Book p200)

questions.q: According to the prevalence-based table, what is advised when trachoma prevalence in 1-9 year old children is more than 10%?
opts: Treatment to affected children and family
Facial cleanliness and environmental change alone
questions.exp: Indications for treatment: > 10% -> mass prophylaxis; 5-10% -> treatment to affected children & family; < 5% -> facial cleanliness & environmental change advised. (Book p200)

questions.q: Match the FISTO grade with its feature — 1) TF  2) TI  3) TS  4) CO  … A) Thickening of upper palpebral conjunctiva  B) > 5 follicles +  C) Arlt's line  D) Visual impairment
questions.exp: FISTO: TF - trachomatous inflammation follicular: > 5 follicles +. TI - trachomatous inflammation intense: thickening of upper palpebral conjunctiva. TS - trachomatous scarring: Arlt's line. CO - corneal opacity: visual impairment. (Book p201)

questions.q: True or false — 'The FISTO table treats the inactive stage of trachoma (TS) with antibiotics.'
opts: False - TS requires surgery, not antibiotics
False - TS (trachomatous scarring) is the inactive stage and needs no treatment; TF and TI are the active stage treated with antibiotics
True - but the antibiotics are given topically only
questions.exp: TS: trachomatous scarring - Arlt's line; inactive stage: no treatment. TF and TI are active stage: treatment - antibiotics. TT requires surgery. (Book p201)

questions.q: In the FISTO table, which grade requires surgery?
opts: TT - trachomatous trichiasis, with eyelash growing inwards
questions.exp: TT: Trachomatous trichiasis - eyelash growing inwards; requires surgery. TF and TI are the active stage (antibiotics); TS is the inactive stage (no treatment). (Book p201)

questions.q: The five photographs of the FISTO classification are captioned trachomatous inflammation follicular, trachomatous inflammation follicular and intense, trachomatous scarring, trachomatous trichiasis and:
questions.exp: Photograph captions: trachomatous inflammation follicular (TF), trachomatous inflammation follicular and intense (TF), trachomatous scarring (TS), trachomatous trichiasis (TT), corneal opacity (CO). (Book p201)

questions.q: Ophthalmia neonatorum is conjunctivitis in neonates with onset within ___ days.
questions.exp: Ophthalmia neonatorum: conjunctivitis in neonates (< 28 days of onset). (Book p201)

questions.q: Match the onset after birth with the cause of ophthalmia neonatorum — 1) Within first 6 h  2) 24 to 48 h  3) 5 to 7 d  … A) HSV-II  B) Chemical conjunctivitis (silver nitrate)  C) Neisseria gonorrhoeae
questions.exp: Causes table: within first 6h - chemical conjunctivitis (silver nitrate); 24 to 48h - Neisseria gonorrhoeae (most severe); 5 to 7 d - HSV-II. (Book p201)

questions.q: Which cause of ophthalmia neonatorum does the table mark as the most severe?
questions.exp: 24 to 48h: Neisseria gonorrhoeae (most severe). (Book p201)

questions.q: Ophthalmia neonatorum developing 2 to 5 days after birth is caused by:
questions.exp: Causes table: 2 to 5 d - other bacteria. (Book p201)

questions.q: A neonate develops conjunctivitis more than 1 week after birth. What is the most common organism?
questions.exp: Causes table: > 1 wk - Chlamydia trachomatis (D to K): m/c. (Book p201)

questions.q: The book's clinical photograph of a neonate with bilateral purulent conjunctivitis illustrates:
questions.exp: Photograph caption: Ophthalmia neonatorum - conjunctivitis in neonates with onset < 28 days. (Book p201)

questions.q: True or false — "Crede's method of prophylaxis (topical 1% silver nitrate) is recommended for the prevention of ophthalmia neonatorum."
opts: True - it is the first choice for prophylaxis
False - it fell out of use because silver nitrate is inactive against gonococci
True - but it is applied only after 1 hour of birth
False - it is not recommended because it causes chemical conjunctivitis
questions.exp: Prevention: 1. Crede's method: topical 1% silver nitrate (not recommended d/t chemical conjunctivitis). (Book p202)

questions.q: For prophylaxis of ophthalmia neonatorum the book advises 0.5% erythromycin or 1% tetracycline as:
opts: A single application within 1 hour of birth
A single application within 6 hours of birth
Three applications on the first day of life
questions.exp: Prevention: 2. 0.5% erythromycin; 3. 1% tetracycline - single application, within 1 hr of birth. (Book p202)

questions.q: Allergic conjunctivitis presents with ___ reaction, watery discharge and itching.
questions.exp: Allergic conjunctivitis: presents with papillae reaction + watery discharge + itching. (Book p202)

questions.q: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis is also known as spring catarrh and is which type of hypersensitivity reaction?
opts: Type I hypersensitivity reaction, eg. pollen
questions.exp: VERNAL KERATOCONJUNCTIVITIS/SPRING CATARRH: Type I hypersensitivity reaction (eg: pollen). (Book p202)

questions.q: Match the incidence feature of vernal keratoconjunctivitis — 1) Age  2) Sex  3) Season  … A) Males > females (young boys)  B) 5-15 yrs  C) m/c in spring & summer
questions.exp: Incidence: age 5-15 yrs; males > females (young boys); m/c in spring & summer; H/O atopy present. (Book p202)

questions.q: Besides age, sex and season, which incidence factor is listed for vernal keratoconjunctivitis?
questions.exp: Incidence: H/O atopy present. (Book p202)

questions.q: Cobble stone papillae of vernal keratoconjunctivitis are due to:
questions.exp: Clinical signs: 1. Papillary hypertrophy: cobble stone papillae. (Book p202)

questions.q: Giant papillae in vernal keratoconjunctivitis are larger than:
questions.exp: Giant papillae: > 1mm size. (Book p202)

questions.q: Horner Trantas sign is a collection of ___ and epithelial debris, situated on the ___.
questions.exp: 2. Horner Trantas sign: collection of eosinophils + epithelial debris; site: on limbus. (Book p202)

questions.q: A child with spring catarrh has a paralimbal grey-white band that resembles arcus senilis. This sign is due to:
opts: Horner Trantas sign from eosinophil collection
questions.exp: 3. Pseudogerontoxon: paralimbal grey-white band (d/t lipid deposition) in children; appearance similar to arcus senilis (photograph labels: Horner trantas sign; Pseudogerontoxon). (Book p202)

questions.q: Which corneal sign is listed in vernal keratoconjunctivitis?
questions.exp: Clinical signs: 4. Shield ulcer (in cornea). (Book p202)

questions.q: Dennie Morgan line in vernal keratoconjunctivitis is an extra ___ crease.
questions.exp: 5. Dennie morgan line: extra lower-lid crease. (Book p202)

questions.q: Maxwell Lyon sign in vernal keratoconjunctivitis is:
questions.exp: 6. Maxwell Lyon sign: ropy discharge. (Book p202)

questions.q: The book warns that excessive itching in vernal keratoconjunctivitis leads to:
questions.exp: Note: excessive itching -> increased incidence of keratoconus. (Book p202)

questions.q: What is the first step in the treatment of vernal keratoconjunctivitis?
questions.exp: Treatment: 1. Cold compress; 2. Topical anti-histamine; 3. Topical mast cell stabilisers; 4. DOC: Olopatadine or Alcaftadine; 5. Topical steroids in acute exacerbation. (Book p203)

questions.q: The drugs of choice (DOC) in vernal keratoconjunctivitis are:
questions.exp: 4. DOC: Olopatadine or Alcaftadine. (Book p203)

questions.q: When are topical steroids used in vernal keratoconjunctivitis?
opts: In acute exacerbation, for symptomatic treatment
questions.exp: 5. Topical steroids in acute exacerbation (for symptomatic treatment). (Book p203)

questions.q: Atopic keratoconjunctivitis is seen in which decades of life?
questions.exp: ATOPIC KERATOCONJUNCTIVITIS: seen in 2nd to 5th decade. (Book p203)

questions.q: An adult with atopic keratoconjunctivitis has lost the lateral part of his eyebrow. This sign is called:
questions.exp: Clinical features: eyelids - Hertoghe sign (lateral eyebrow lost). (Book p203)

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed among the clinical features of atopic keratoconjunctivitis?
questions.exp: AKC clinical features: eyelids - Hertoghe sign (lateral eyebrow lost); itching; papillae; watery discharge. (Ropy discharge is the Maxwell Lyon sign of VKC.) (Book p203)

questions.q: Treatment of atopic keratoconjunctivitis is topical anti-histamine and:
opts: Surgical excision of the lid lesion
questions.exp: AKC treatment: 1. Topical anti-histamine; 2. Topical mast cell stabilisers. (Book p203)

questions.q: Giant papillary keratoconjunctivitis has papillae > 1 mm and which type of hypersensitivity reaction?
questions.exp: GIANT PAPILLARY KERATOCONJUNCTIVITIS: papillae > 1mm; Type IV hypersensitivity reaction. (Book p203)

questions.q: Giant papillary keratoconjunctivitis is mechanically induced by all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Etiology of GPC: mechanically induced by contact lens, ocular prostheses, protruding sutures. (Book p203)

questions.q: Treatment of giant papillary keratoconjunctivitis is:
opts: Observation only, as it always resolves spontaneously
Anti-histamine plus surgery to remove the irritant (if required)
questions.exp: Treatment: anti-histamine + surgery to remove irritant (if required). (Book p203)

questions.q: Phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis is a Type IV hypersensitivity reaction in response to:
questions.exp: PHYLCTENULAR KERATOCONJUNCTIVITIS: Type IV hypersensitivity reaction in response to endogenous allergen. (Book p203)

questions.q: Match the region with the most common cause of phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis — 1) India  2) Western countries  … A) Staphylococcus aureus  B) TB
questions.exp: Etiology: m/c in India - TB; m/c in western countries - Staphylococcus aureus. (Book p203)

questions.q: A phlycten is a nodule located near the:
questions.exp: Clinical features: phlycten - nodule near limbus (photograph caption: Phlycten). (Book p203)

questions.q: A phlycten grows towards the cornea and ulcerates. Which ulcers does the flow chart say it gives rise to?
questions.exp: Phlycten -> grows towards cornea -> ulcerates -> gives rise to sacrofulous ulcer, fascicular ulcer, miliary ulcer. (Book p203)

questions.q: Treatment of phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis is:
questions.exp: Treatment: topical steroids. (Book p203)

questions.q: Pterygium is a triangular, ___ growth of degenerative sub-conjunctival tissue over the cornea.
questions.exp: Pterygium: triangular, fibrovascular growth of degenerative sub-conjunctival tissue over cornea (photographs of pterygium). (Book p204)

questions.q: Pterygium destroys which layers of the cornea?
opts: Full-thickness stroma up to the endothelium
questions.exp: Pterygium destroys Bowman's layer & superficial stroma. (Book p204)

questions.q: Pterygium is associated with all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Pterygium is associated with UV ray exposure, dust, humidity. (Book p204)

questions.q: The cause of pterygium is limbal stem cell deficiency leading to:
opts: Deposition of iron in the cornea
Deposition of lipid in the paralimbal area
questions.exp: Cause: limbal stem cell deficiency -> activation of matrix metalloproteinase. (Book p204)

questions.q: Pterygium is more common on which side?
questions.exp: Site: Nasal > Lateral. (Book p204)

questions.q: In pterygium the triangular growth has its apex towards the ___.
questions.exp: Clinical features: 1. Triangular growth with apex towards cornea. (Book p204)

questions.q: Stocker's line in pterygium is:
opts: Deposition of iron in front of the apex
Deposition of lipid in the paralimbal area
An extra crease of the lower lid
questions.exp: 2. Stocker's line: deposition of iron in front of apex. (Book p204)

questions.q: A pterygium is reducing a patient's vision. According to the book this is due to corneal astigmatism or:
opts: Encroaching into the visual axis (covering the pupillary area)
Deposition of iron in front of the apex
questions.exp: Loss of vision in pterygium: a. corneal astigmatism; b. encroaching into visual axis (the photograph is labelled 'covers pupillary area'). (Book p204)

questions.q: What is the drawback of surgical excision of pterygium?
opts: It causes loss of the eyelid margin
It increases the rate of recurrence
questions.exp: Treatment: surgical excision - increased rate of recurrence. (Book p204)

questions.q: Which topical agent is used to reduce recurrence after pterygium excision?
questions.exp: To reduce recurrence: 1. Topical mitomycin C; 2. Autograft. (Book p204)

questions.q: The autograft used to reduce recurrence after pterygium excision is harvested from:
opts: The other eye, usually from the superior site
The same eye, usually from the superior site, and fixed with sutures, fibrin glue or autologous serum
The buccal mucosa, fixed with sutures
The same eye, usually from the inferior fornix
questions.exp: Autograft: harvested from same eye; site: usually superior; fixed with sutures/fibrin glue/autologous serum. (Book p204)

questions.q: Pinguecula is ___ degeneration of collagen fibres in the stroma of the conjunctiva.
questions.exp: Heading: Pinguecula & concretions. PINGUECULA: elastic degeneration of collagen fibres in stroma of conjunctiva. (Book p205)

questions.q: What is the most common site of pinguecula?
questions.exp: m/c site: nasal part of conjunctiva. (Book p205)

questions.q: A yellowish fat-like nodule is seen on the conjunctiva away from the cornea. The photograph on this page labels it as:
questions.exp: Photograph caption (pinguecula): yellowish fat-like nodules. (Book p205)

questions.q: Concretions are a collection of ___ and mucus.
questions.exp: CONCRETIONS: collection of epithelial debris & mucus. (Book p205)

questions.q: Concretions are caused by irritation due to friction of the eyelid against the bulbar conjunctiva and cornea while:
opts: Rubbing the eye with the knuckles
questions.exp: Cause: irritation d/t friction of eyelid against bulbar conjunctiva & cornea while blinking. (Book p205)

questions.q: How are concretions removed?
opts: By surgical excision under local anaesthesia
questions.exp: Treatment: Removel with 26g needle. (Also: spontaneously resolves with good lubrication.) (Book p205)

questions.q: True or false — 'Concretions contain calcium deposits.'
opts: True - they are calcific deposits in the conjunctiva
False - they contain lipid deposits instead of calcium
True - they contain calcium and mucus
False - the note states that concretions do not contain calcium deposits
questions.exp: Note: Concretions do not contain calcium deposits. (Book p205)

questions.q: The photograph of concretions on this page shows minute ___ elevations.
questions.exp: Photograph caption (concretions): minute yellowish-white elevations. (Book p205)

units.title: Anatomy of conjunctiva: parts
units.guide: Conjunctiva = transparent mucous membrane that does not cover the cornea; bulbar, forniceal and palpebral parts; plica semilunaris (nictitating membrane) and caruncle (hair follicles) as rudimentary structures.

units.title: Histology of the conjunctiva
units.guide: Outermost epithelium = non-keratinised stratified squamous with goblet cells (mucin, innermost tear-film layer, parasympathetic), melanocytes and Langerhans cells; adenoid/lymphatic layer develops after 3 months; fibrous layer carries nerves and vessels.

units.title: Lymphatic drainage of the conjunctiva
units.guide: Conjunctiva is the only site of lymphatic drainage from the eye: medially to submandibular nodes, laterally to peri-auricular and superficial parotid nodes.

units.title: Conjunctivitis: symptoms and signs
units.guide: Aka eye flu: redness, discharge sticking to eyelids, foreign body sensation, lacrimation, itching (if allergic), pain and LOV (corneal involvement); conjunctival vs circumcorneal hyperemia and its differential diagnosis.

units.title: Other conjunctival signs and inflammatory reactions
units.guide: Subconjunctival hemorrhage needs no treatment; chemosis = swelling of bulbar conjunctiva; discharge causes colored halos and stickiness; papillae = hypertrophied vessels, follicles = lymphoid aggregates; discharge-to-reaction etiology table.

units.title: Bacterial conjunctivitis: purulent, membranous and angular
units.guide: Blenorrhoea (N. gonorrhoeae, oculogenital, ceftriaxone + erythromycin); membranous (Pneumococcus/diphtheria, membrane fuses and bleeds) vs pseudomembranous (no fusion, no bleeding); angular conjunctivitis (Moraxella, excoriation at canthi, tetracycline + zinc boric).

units.title: Viral conjunctivitis
units.guide: Adenoviral: non-specific follicular (1-11, 19), EKC (8, 19, 37), PCF (3, 4, 7 with preauricular lymphadenopathy); Apollo/acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis (Coxsackie A24 m/c, enterovirus 70, adenovirus 11); molluscum contagiosum nodule.

units.title: Chlamydial conjunctivitis and trachoma
units.guide: Chlamydia serovars (adult inclusion D-K; trachoma A, B, Ba, C; ophthalmia neonatorum D-K); trachoma = Egyptian ophthalmia, 3F transmission; Type IV hypersensitivity; sago grain follicles with Leber cells; Arlt's line, Herbert's pits, pannus; SAFE strategy and the prevalence-based treatment table.

units.title: FISTO classification (WHO)
units.guide: TF (>5 follicles, active, antibiotics), TI (thickening of upper palpebral conjunctiva, active), TS (Arlt's line, inactive, no treatment), TT (eyelash growing inwards, surgery), CO (corneal opacity, visual impairment).

units.title: Ophthalmia neonatorum: causes and prophylaxis
units.guide: Conjunctivitis in neonates (<28 days of onset); causes by onset - chemical/silver nitrate (6 h), gonococcus (24-48 h, most severe), other bacteria (2-5 d), HSV-II (5-7 d), Chlamydia D-K (>1 wk, m/c); prophylaxis - Crede's silver nitrate (not recommended), erythromycin 0.5%/tetracycline 1% single application within 1 hour of birth.

units.title: Allergic conjunctivitis: vernal keratoconjunctivitis
units.guide: Allergic conjunctivitis = papillary reaction + watery discharge + itching; VKC/spring catarrh, Type I hypersensitivity (pollen), 5-15 yrs, boys, spring and summer, atopy; cobble stone/giant papillae, Horner Trantas sign, pseudogerontoxon, shield ulcer, Dennie Morgan line, Maxwell Lyon sign, keratoconus risk; treatment ladder.

units.title: Atopic, giant papillary and phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis
units.guide: AKC (2nd-5th decade, Hertoghe sign, anti-histamine + mast cell stabilisers); GPC (papillae >1 mm, Type IV, contact lens/prostheses/sutures, anti-histamine + removal of irritant); phlyctenular KC (Type IV to endogenous allergen, TB in India, S. aureus in the west, phlycten near limbus ulcerating into sacrofulous/fascicular/miliary ulcers, topical steroids).

units.title: Pterygium
units.guide: Triangular fibrovascular growth over the cornea destroying Bowman's layer and superficial stroma; UV, dust, humidity; limbal stem cell deficiency with matrix metalloproteinase activation; nasal > lateral; Stocker's line; loss of vision; excision with mitomycin C and autograft.

units.title: Pinguecula and concretions
units.guide: Pinguecula = elastic degeneration of collagen fibres in the conjunctival stroma, commonest nasally, yellowish fat-like nodules; concretions = epithelial debris and mucus from friction while blinking, removed with a 26g needle, resolve with lubrication, contain no calcium.
